explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Secondhand would be hearing it through somebody else. The writer says the Word of life is “…which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands…” (1 John 1:1). That's a front-row seat, with no middleman at all.

You got it, baker. The writer says they heard it, saw it with their own eyes, gazed upon it and touched it with their own hands (1 John 1:1). That's a front-row seat, and I think he'd have been a little offended by the word secondhand.

explanations.answer: They testify to it and proclaim it
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The writer says, “we have seen it and testified to it, and we proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us.” They saw it, and then they spoke up about it. When you've seen something that big, sitting on it is not really an option.

explanations.answer: They keep it quiet among themselves
explanations.explanation: Close the oven door on that one, baker. The text says the opposite. The writer says they testified to it and proclaim it to the readers (1 John 1:2). Nothing in this verse has them hushing up.

explanations.answer: They wait for the right time to share it
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, baker, but the verse doesn't mention any waiting. It says, “we have seen it and testified to it, and we proclaim to you…” (1 John 1:2). They're already testifying, and they're proclaiming it right there in the letter.

explanations.answer: So the readers can have fellowship with them
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. The writer says, “We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us.” (1 John 1:3). He's opening the door and inviting the readers in. He also says they write so that their joy may be complete (1 John 1:4).

explanations.answer: So the readers can earn a place among them
explanations.explanation: Not this time, baker. Look at how the verse puts it: “…so that you also may have fellowship with us.” (1 John 1:3). The writer says nothing about earning anything. He just says they proclaim it so the readers may share in the fellowship.

explanations.answer: So the readers can prove they are worthy
explanations.explanation: Nope, baker, nobody's handing out a test here. The verse gives the reason: “…so that you also may have fellowship with us.” (1 John 1:3). Proving worth doesn't show up anywhere in it.

That's right, baker. The writer says, “And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ.” (1 John 1:3). Two names, and both are the very top of the list. You can't get better company than that.

Back to the dough on this one, baker. The verse says, “And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ.” (1 John 1:3). So the statement is true, and the writer really does say it. I'd read that line one more time just to enjoy it.
Yes, baker. The writer says, “We write these things so that our joy may be complete.” (1 John 1:4). Joy is the word he picks. It's a pretty good reason to pick up a pen.
Easy to see why that tempts you, baker. Writing a letter is work, after all. But the verse says, “We write these things so that our joy may be complete.” (1 John 1:4). The word is joy.
Good guess, baker, because a message is coming up soon. But verse 4 says, “We write these things so that our joy may be complete.” (1 John 1:4). Joy is the word that fits in the blank.
That's it, baker. The writer says, “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.” (1 John 1:5). Notice the words “at all.” He doesn't leave even a little dark corner.

Not this time, baker. The writer says, “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.” (1 John 1:5). So the statement is true, and he says it plainly. I'd pop a cookie in the oven and read it again.

explanations.answer: We lie and don't practice the truth
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The writer says, “If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.” (1 John 1:6). What we say and how we walk have to match. Otherwise the words and the walk are telling two different stories.

explanations.answer: We lose the joy we were given
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The verse never mentions losing joy. It says, “…we lie and do not practice the truth.” (1 John 1:6). That's the writer's verdict when the words and the walk don't match.

explanations.answer: We are cut off and can't return
explanations.explanation: Hold on, baker, that's heavier than the text. Verse 6 says, “…we lie and do not practice the truth.” It doesn't say anything about being cut off. And a few verses later the writer says, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins…” (1 John 1:9).

explanations.answer: The blood of Jesus His Son
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says, “…the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin.” (1 John 1:7). Notice the words “all sin.” It's no partial clean-up.

explanations.answer: The water of the Jordan River
explanations.explanation: Nice try, baker, but that's not what the writer names. He says, “…the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin.” (1 John 1:7). The cleansing comes from Jesus, not from any river.

explanations.answer: The ashes of a red heifer
explanations.explanation: Interesting pick, baker, but it isn't in this letter. The verse says, “…the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin.” (1 John 1:7). Jesus is the one named as doing the cleansing.

Flip that around, baker. The writer says, “But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another…” (1 John 1:7). Walking in the light brings fellowship with one another. It doesn't take it away.

That's right, baker. The writer says, “…if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another…” (1 John 1:7). Walking in the light goes with fellowship, not with losing it. A good kitchen is better when it's full of people.

That's right, baker. The writer says, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” (1 John 1:8). The one who gets fooled is the one doing the saying. Quite a plot twist.
Close, baker, but the verse points the finger back at us. It says, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves…” (1 John 1:8). The one deceived is the person making the claim.
Not this time, baker. The writer says, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” (1 John 1:8). Our leaders aren't in this verse. It's about whoever says it.

Hang on, baker, because that's not what the text says. The writer says, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9). There's no making up for it first. The forgiveness comes with the confessing.

Yes, baker. The writer says, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9). No makeup work is listed, and no payment plan either. He is faithful and just to forgive.

Right, baker. The writer says, “If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar, and His word is not in us.” (1 John 1:10). Saying we've never sinned puts us at odds with what God says. That's a bad spot to bake yourself into.
Good try, baker, but the verse picks a sharper word. It says, “If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar…” (1 John 1:10). The word is liar, not stranger.

Not that one, baker. The writer says, “If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar, and His word is not in us.” (1 John 1:10). Nobody is standing on the sidelines in this verse. The word that fits is liar.

That's it, baker. The writer says, “But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One.” (1 John 2:1). An advocate is someone who stands up for you. When we sin, we aren't left to speak for ourselves.
That's not the name the writer gives, baker. He says our advocate before the Father is “…Jesus Christ, the Righteous One.” (1 John 2:1). The text puts Jesus in that spot.

Not this one, baker. The text names a different advocate. The writer says, “…we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One.” (1 John 2:1). Jesus stands before the Father for us.

You've got it, baker. The writer says Jesus “…is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.” (1 John 2:2). That's a big reach, and I can't think of a bigger circle to draw. It doesn't stop with the writer and his readers.
Close, baker, but the writer opens the circle wider. He says, “…not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.” (1 John 2:2). It doesn't stop with the ones who saw Him.
Not quite, baker. The verse never ties it to keeping the Law. The writer says, “…not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.” (1 John 2:2). The circle reaches the whole world.
